_note: Recording text for ElevenLabs v3 (Building, English). Paste these into ElevenLabs instead of the plain panel text. Tag rules from the story bible: one emotion tag at the start of the words it colours, [pause] right before a punchline or key term, at most 3 or 4 tags per line; regenerate any take that reads a tag aloud. Words are only respelled where a voice would misread a symbol (___ , ÷ , Xs, A and a). Beginning lines: no tags, slower pace.
A0.title.body: [warm] A story about a newt who regrows her tail, [pause] and what that tells us about every cell in her body. Press Next to begin.
A0.story.body: [friendly] Listen to the story, or read the captions. The arrows on the caption bar go line by line.
A0.regrow.body: [curious] Step through the weeks and watch the tail come back: stump, [pause] bud, [pause] half a tail, [pause] the whole tail.
A0.P1.prompt: [curious] Fig's new tail has bone, muscle, skin, and even the stripes. Where do you think her body got the instructions to build it? [pause] Write your prediction.
frame.predict: [encouraging] I think Fig's body knew how to build the tail because [pause] blank.
ui.retrieve.intro: [warm] Write what you remember. Then show the answer, and check yourself.
A1.R1.prompt: [curious] What is the smallest unit that is alive?
A1.R2.prompt: [curious] Name one part that plant cells have, and animal cells do not.
A1.R3.prompt: [curious] What does the cell membrane do?
A1.R4.prompt: [curious] In the story, what grew back after the heron's attack?
A1.zoom.body: [warm] Use the zoom buttons to go from Fig down to her DNA, one level at a time.
A1.zoom.fig.text: [warm] This is Fig. Her new tail is where we're going.
A1.zoom.tissue.text: A slice of tail: skin on the outside, muscle, and bone in the middle. [pause] Each layer is a tissue, made of cells.
A1.zoom.cell.text: One tail cell. The big round part in the middle [pause] is the nucleus.
A1.zoom.nucleus.text: Inside the nucleus are the chromosomes. [curious] Most of the time they're long, loose threads, tangled together. Our model newt has four.
A1.zoom.chromosome.text: One chromosome: a long piece of DNA. Before a cell divides, each thread coils up tight into a short, thick chromosome [pause] like this one.
A1.zoom.gene.text: The highlighted band is one gene. [pause] One chromosome carries many genes.
A1.zoom.dna.text: [impressed] Unwind the chromosome and you find DNA: two long strands twisted round each other, joined by pairs that fit together [pause] like puzzle pieces.
A1.pairs.body1: The two long chromosomes are one pair. The two short ones are the other pair. In each pair, M, the solid paper, came from the mother, [pause] and P, the striped paper, came from the father.
A1.pairs.body2: Partners carry the same genes in the same places, and they share the same pattern of light bands. The letters show versions: [pause] capital A and small a are two versions of the same gene.
A1.copy.body1: Before a cell divides, it copies every chromosome. [pause] Step through the copying, and watch the count strip.
A1.copy.body2: The number of chromosomes stays at four. [pause] The number of DNA molecules goes from four to eight.
A1.W1.prompt: [teacherly] Watch how to count chromosomes and DNA molecules in a cell that has copied its DNA.
A1.W1.step1: [teacherly] Find the centromeres: the dot where the two halves of each X are joined. [pause] Each centromere marks one chromosome.
A1.W1.step2: Count them: one, two, three, four. [pause] This cell has four chromosomes.
A1.W1.step3: Now count the halves of the X's. [pause] Each half is one DNA molecule.
A1.W1.step4: Four chromosomes, with two halves each, make [pause] eight DNA molecules.
A1.G1.prompt: This cell hasn't copied its DNA yet. [pause] Count the chromosomes and the DNA molecules.
A1.G1.step1: Count the centromeres, the dots, to count chromosomes.
A1.G1.step2: Each single rod is one DNA molecule.
A1.G1.hint1: [helpful] Each chromosome has one centromere: [pause] the dot.
A1.G1.hint2: [helpful] A single rod hasn't been copied, so it's [pause] one DNA molecule.
A1.G1.fb.correct: [pleased] Four chromosomes, four DNA molecules. [pause] Before copying, the two counts match.
fb.pairsCountedAsOne: [gently] You counted pairs. A pair is two chromosomes, [pause] so count every rod or X on its own.
mis.pairsCountedAsOne: A pair counts as one chromosome.
fb.dnaDoublesAlways: [gently] These rods haven't been copied yet. [pause] One single rod is one DNA molecule.
mis.dnaDoublesAlways: Every chromosome holds two DNA molecules.
fb.recount: [encouraging] Count again. Touch each centromere, the dot, once for chromosomes. [pause] Then count every rod, or half of an X, for DNA molecules.
A1.G2.prompt: Match each chromosome with its partner. [pause] Select one, then select its partner.
A1.G2.step1: Look for two chromosomes that are the same length, and carry the same gene letters.
hint.pair1: [helpful] Partners are the same length, have the same pattern of light bands, and carry the same genes: [pause] the same letter, capital or small.
hint.pair2: [helpful] Each pair has one M, solid paper, [pause] and one P, striped paper.
A1.G2.fb.correct: [pleased] Both pairs matched: same genes, [pause] one from each parent.
fb.pairSameParent: [gently] Those two both came from the same parent. [pause] A pair is one from the mother, M, and one from the father, P.
mis.pairSameParent: Both chromosomes in a pair come from the same parent.
fb.pairByLook: [gently] Those two carry different genes: look at the length and the letters. Partners are the same length, with the same gene letters, [pause] even if the versions differ, like capital A and small a.
mis.pairByLook: Any two chromosomes can be partners.
ui.task.revealPairs: [kindly] Here are the pairs. Each pair is the same length, with the same gene letters: [pause] one M and one P.
A1.G3.prompt: These chromosomes have been copied. [pause] Count the chromosomes and the DNA molecules.
A1.G3.step2: Count the halves of the X's for DNA molecules.
hint.x1: [helpful] An X is one chromosome that has been copied. [pause] It has one centromere.
hint.x2: [helpful] Each X has two halves. [pause] Each half is one DNA molecule.
A1.G3.fb.correct: [pleased] Four chromosomes, eight DNA molecules. [pause] Copying doubles the DNA, not the number of chromosomes.
fb.xIsTwoChromosomes: [gently] You counted each half of an X as a chromosome. An X is one chromosome, [pause] copied. Count centromeres, not arms.
fb.xIsOneDna: [gently] Each X holds two DNA molecules, one in each half. [pause] Count the halves.
mis.xIsOneDna: An X is one DNA molecule.
A1.I1.prompt: Count the chromosomes and the DNA molecules in this cell.
A1.I1.fb.correct: [pleased] Four chromosomes and eight DNA molecules, [pause] however they're turned.
A1.I1GF.prompt: [curious] A cell has twelve DNA molecules, and every chromosome in it is an X. [pause] How many chromosomes does it have?
A1.I1GF.fb12: [gently] Twelve is the number of DNA molecules. Each X holds two of them, [pause] so there are fewer chromosomes than that.
A1.I1GF.fb6: [pleased] Twelve DNA molecules, divided by two per X, [pause] makes six chromosomes.
A1.I1GF.fb3: [gently] Three is the number of pairs. [pause] Each pair is two chromosomes.
A1.I1GF.fb24: [gently] Copying doubles the DNA, not the chromosomes. [pause] Divide by two instead.
mis.copyDoublesChromosomes: Copying doubles the number of chromosomes.
A1.I2.prompt: These chromosomes have been copied. [pause] Match each one with its partner.
A1.I2.fb.correct: [pleased] Matched. Copied or not, partners have the same genes, [pause] and come from different parents.
A1.I3.prompt: [curious] Which of these is a gene?
A1.I3.hint1: [helpful] Think back to the zoom: chromosome, [pause] then gene, [pause] then DNA.
A1.I3.fbChromosome: [gently] A chromosome holds many genes. [pause] A gene is only one section of it.
mis.geneIsChromosome: A gene is a whole chromosome.
A1.I3.fbChromatid: [gently] Each half of an X is a whole DNA molecule, [pause] with many genes on it.
mis.geneIsChromatid: A gene is one half of an X.
A1.I3.fbSection: [pleased] A gene is a section of a chromosome, [pause] like one recipe in a cookbook.
A1.I3.fbCell: [gently] Cells hold chromosomes, [pause] and genes are sections of chromosomes.
mis.geneIsCell: A gene is a kind of cell.
A1.check.body: [encouraging] Three questions about cells from a different animal. [pause] Show what you know on your own: hints and worked steps are off.
A1.C1.prompt: This cell comes from a different animal. [pause] Count its chromosomes and DNA molecules.
ui.task.firstTry: [calm] Saved. Your first answer counts for the checkpoint.
A1.C2.prompt: Match the chromosomes from this animal into pairs.
A1.C3.prompt: [curious] What is true about the two chromosomes in a pair?
A1.C3.optCopies: They are exact copies of each other.
A1.C3.fbCopies: [gently] Exact copies are the two halves of an X. Partners come from two parents, [pause] so their versions can differ.
mis.pairIsCopy: The two chromosomes in a pair are exact copies.
A1.C3.optMother: Both of them come from the mother.
A1.C3.fbMother: [gently] One partner comes from the mother, [pause] and one from the father.
A1.C3.fbDifferent: [gently] Partners carry the same genes, [pause] in the same places.
A1.C3.optSame: They carry the same genes, but versions can differ.
A1.C3.fbSame: [pleased] Same genes, and the versions can differ, [pause] like capital A and small a.
A1.end.body1: [warm] Genes are sections of chromosomes. [pause] Chromosomes come in pairs, one from each parent.
A1.end.body2: An X is one chromosome, copied: one chromosome, two DNA molecules. [pause] [curious] Next: how does one cell become two?
frame.count: [encouraging] There are blank chromosomes because blank. [pause] There are blank DNA molecules because blank.
frame.pair: [encouraging] These two are partners because blank.
A2.R1.prompt: [curious] How many DNA molecules are in one X-shaped chromosome?
A2.R2.prompt: [curious] Where do the two chromosomes in a pair come from?
A2.R4.prompt: [curious] Name one reason a living thing needs to make new cells.
A2.intro.body1: [warm] Fig's tail grows back because cells divide: one cell becomes two. [pause] Each new cell needs exactly what the parent cell had.
A2.intro.body2: [warm] Next, try it your way. You can copy the chromosomes first, or not. [pause] Mistakes are fine: you will see what happens.
A2.T1.prompt: [warm] Give each new cell everything the parent cell had. Select a chromosome, then a new cell. [pause] When the parent cell is empty, divide it.
A2.T1.fb.correct: [pleased] Both new cells match the parent. How did you get there? [pause] Next, watch how real cells do it.
A2.fb.missing: [gently] A new cell is missing a chromosome. [pause] Without copying first, there is only one of each chromosome to share, so one cell has to go without.
mis.divideWithoutCopy: A cell can divide without copying first.
A2.fb.extra: [gently] A new cell has an extra chromosome, and the other is missing it. [pause] Both halves of one X went to the same cell: send one half to each.
mis.bothHalvesOneCell: Both halves of an X can go to the same new cell.
A2.fb.mixed: [gently] The new cells don't match the parent: some chromosomes are doubled and some are missing. [pause] Each new cell needs one copy of every chromosome.
mis.splitByParent: One new cell gets the mother's chromosomes and the other gets the father's.
A2.mitosis.body1: [warm] Step through and watch the count strip. [pause] First, every chromosome is copied: each one becomes an X, with two identical halves.
A2.mitosis.body2: [warm] Then the X's line up, and fibres pull the two halves of every X to opposite ends. [pause] One half of each X goes to each new cell.
A2.mitosis.body3: [warm] That is why the copy comes first: without it, there would be only one of each chromosome to share. [pause] This whole process is called mitosis.
A2.G1.prompt: [warm] Now divide this cell the way real cells do. [pause] Copy first, then send one half of each X to each new cell.
A2.G1.step1: [teacherly] Press "Copy the chromosomes". [pause] Every chromosome becomes an X.
A2.G1.step2: [teacherly] Select an X and put it in new cell one: [pause] one half goes there, and the other half stays to be placed.
A2.G1.step3: [teacherly] Put that other half in new cell two. [pause] Do the same for every X, then divide.
A2.hint1: [helpful] Copy before you divide: [pause] each new cell needs its own copy of every chromosome.
A2.hint2: [helpful] Each X gives one half to each new cell. [pause] Never send both halves to the same cell.
frame.divide: [encouraging] Each new cell has the same chromosomes as the parent because blank.
A2.G1.fb.correct: [pleased] Each new cell has one copy of every chromosome: [pause] the same information as the parent.
A2.I1.prompt: [warm] This cell is from a different animal, with three pairs. [pause] Divide it so both new cells match the parent.
A2.I1.fb.correct: [pleased] Six chromosomes in each new cell, one copy of each, just like the parent.
A2.GF.prompt: [curious] A human skin cell has forty-six chromosomes. It divides by mitosis. [pause] What do the two new cells have?
A2.GF.hint: [helpful] Mitosis gives each new cell the same information as the parent.
A2.GF.fb23: [gently] Halving happens when eggs and sperm are made, not in mitosis. [pause] Mitosis keeps the full set.
mis.mitosisHalves: Mitosis halves the number of chromosomes.
A2.GF.fb92: [gently] The copy is shared between the two cells, so the number does not double.
A2.GF.opt46: Forty-six chromosomes each, the same as the parent.
A2.GF.fb46: [pleased] Mitosis copies all forty-six, then shares them: [pause] each new cell gets the full set.
A2.GF.opt46diff: Forty-six chromosomes each, but different genes.
A2.GF.fb46diff: [gently] Each half of an X is an exact copy, so both cells carry the same genes.
mis.daughtersDiffer: The two new cells get different genes.
A2.I2.prompt: [curious] A cell divides. One new cell gets three chromosomes; the other gets five. The parent had four. [pause] What went wrong?
A2.I2.hint: [helpful] Three + five equals eight: the cell did copy. [pause] Where did the halves of the X's go?
A2.I2.optNoCopy: The cell forgot to copy its chromosomes.
A2.I2.fbNoCopy: [gently] Without copying there would be only four chromosomes to share, not eight.
A2.I2.optBoth: Both halves of one X went into the same cell.
A2.I2.fbBoth: [pleased] One X sent both halves to one cell: [pause] that cell got an extra, and the other is missing one.
A2.I2.optExtraCopy: The cell copied one chromosome twice.
A2.I2.fbExtraCopy: [gently] Then there would be nine halves, not eight. [pause] The count is right; the sharing went wrong.
A2.I2.optNormal: Nothing; new cells are often different.
A2.I2.fbNormal: [gently] Mitosis makes two cells that match the parent. [pause] A cell missing a chromosome has a problem.
A2.check.body: [encouraging] Three questions about cells dividing. [pause] Show what you know on your own: hints and worked steps are off.
A2.C1.prompt: [warm] Divide this cell from a different animal so both new cells match the parent.
A2.C1.fb.correct: [pleased] Both new cells match the parent.
A2.C2.prompt: [curious] After mitosis, how does the DNA in each new cell compare with the parent cell's DNA?
A2.C2.optHalf: Each new cell has half of the parent's DNA.
A2.C2.fbHalf: [gently] Mitosis copies first, so each cell gets a full set.
A2.C2.optDiffer: The two new cells have different genes.
A2.C2.fbDiffer: [gently] The two halves of each X are exact copies, so both cells get the same genes.
A2.C2.optDouble: Each new cell has twice as many chromosomes.
A2.C2.fbDouble: [gently] The copies are shared out, one half to each cell, so the number stays the same.
A2.C2.optSame: Each new cell has the same DNA as the parent.
A2.C2.fbSame: [pleased] Same DNA, same chromosomes: [pause] two identical copies of the parent cell.
A2.C3.prompt: [curious] Before dividing, a cell has six chromosomes, and each one is an X. [pause] After mitosis, what does each new cell have?
A2.C3.fb6and6: [pleased] Each new cell gets one half of each X: [pause] six single chromosomes, six DNA molecules.
A2.C3.fb3and6: [gently] Mitosis does not halve the chromosomes: [pause] every new cell gets one of each of the six.
A2.C3.fb6and12: [gently] The X's are pulled apart, so the new cells get single halves, not whole X's.
mis.daughtersKeepX: The new cells keep whole X-shaped chromosomes.
A2.C3.fb12and12: [gently] An X is one chromosome, copied. [pause] Its halves are shared between the two cells.
A2.end.body1: [warm] Mitosis copies every chromosome, then pulls the copies apart so each new cell gets one of each.
A2.end.body2: [warm] The two new cells have the same DNA as each other and as the parent. [pause] Next: how long does each part of this take?
A2b.R1.prompt: [curious] What happens to every chromosome before a cell divides?
A2b.R2.prompt: [curious] After mitosis, how do the two new cells compare with the parent cell?
A2b.R4.prompt: [curious] What does the nucleus of a cell hold?
A2b.cycle.body1: [warm] A dividing cell goes round and round a cycle. [pause] The slices show how much of the cycle each part takes: interphase is most of it.
A2b.cycle.body2: [warm] The cycle is continuous: one part flows into the next. [pause] The five names are lines that scientists drew to talk about it; the cell does not stop between them.
A2b.slide.body: [warm] Each cell on the slide was caught at one moment of its cycle. [pause] If you count how many cells are in each part, you can work out how long each part takes.
A2b.W1.prompt: [warm] Watch the first three cells being sorted. [pause] The cards show what to look for.
A2b.W1.step1: [teacherly] Cell one: a round, dark nucleus and no chromosomes you can see. [pause] That is interphase.
A2b.W1.step2: [teacherly] Cell two: chromosomes lined up across the middle. [pause] That is metaphase.
A2b.W1.step3: [teacherly] Cell three: two sets of chromosomes pulling apart. [pause] That is anaphase.
A2b.G1.prompt: [warm] Now you sort the six cells in rings. [pause] Choose a card, click the cells that match, then check.
A2b.hint.sort1: [helpful] Look for a nucleus first. A round, dark nucleus with no threads: interphase. [pause] A paler nucleus with threads: prophase.
A2b.hint.sort2: [helpful] No nucleus? [pause] Look at the chromosomes: one line in the middle is metaphase; two sets moving apart is anaphase; two new nuclei is telophase.
A2b.I1.prompt: [warm] Sort the rest of the slide on your own. [pause] Then check: your counts go into the next step.
A2b.T1.step1: [teacherly] Example: [pause] if three of thirty-six cells are in metaphase, the share is three divided by thirty-six equals about eight percent.
A2b.T1.step2: [teacherly] The share of cells is the share of time. [pause] Eight percent of twenty-four hours is zero point zero eight times twenty-four equals about two hours.
A2b.T1.step3: [teacherly] Do the same for every phase. [pause] Your counts may differ from a classmate's: each slide is different.
A2b.hint.time1: [helpful] Share of cells equals cells in the phase divided by all cells, times one hundred.
A2b.hint.time2: [helpful] Hours equals share times twenty-four. [pause] Check: all the hours together should add up to about twenty-four.
A2b.T1.fb.correct: [pleased] Your table is right. [pause] Interphase takes most of the day; the parts of mitosis take an hour or two each.
A2b.I2.prompt: [curious] In your slide, which phase takes the longest? [pause] How do you know?
A2b.I2.hint: [helpful] More cells caught in a phase means cells spend more time in it.
A2b.I2.optFewest: The phase with the fewest cells, because those cells finished fast.
A2b.I2.fbFewest: [gently] Few cells in a phase means cells pass through it quickly, so it is short.
mis.moreCellsFaster: A phase with more cells is a faster phase.
A2b.I2.optMost: The phase with the most cells, because cells spend longest there.
A2b.I2.fbMost: [pleased] A phase with more cells lasts longer: [pause] a cell is more likely to be caught in it.
A2b.I2.optSame: They all take the same time; the slide is random.
A2b.I2.fbSame: [gently] If every phase took the same time, the counts would be about equal. [pause] They are not.
mis.phasesEqual: Every phase takes the same amount of time.
A2b.I2.optResting: Interphase, because the cell is resting.
A2b.I2.fbResting: [gently] Interphase is longest, but not because the cell rests: [pause] it grows and copies its DNA then.
A2b.GF.prompt: [curious] A chemical stops cells from moving past metaphase. [pause] After a few hours, what happens to the counts on a slide?
A2b.GF.hint: [helpful] Cells keep arriving at metaphase, but none leave.
A2b.GF.optPile: Metaphase cells pile up, and anaphase and telophase cells disappear.
A2b.GF.fbPile: [pleased] Cells flow into metaphase and get stuck, so they pile up there. [pause] Controlling when cells move on is how bodies control growth.
A2b.GF.optNone: Nothing changes; each phase is separate.
A2b.GF.fbNone: [gently] The phases are connected: [pause] blocking one backs up the cells behind it.
mis.phasesSeparate: The phases are separate steps that don't affect each other.
A2b.GF.optSame: All five counts stay the same.
A2b.GF.fbSame: [gently] Cells still flow in, but none flow out, so the metaphase count grows.
A2b.GF.optInter: Interphase disappears, because metaphase is now faster.
A2b.GF.fbInter: [gently] Cells still leave interphase as usual; they just cannot get past metaphase.
A2b.O1.prompt: [warm] This slide comes from Fig's old tail. [pause] Sort every cell, then check.
A2b.O2.prompt: [curious] Almost every cell in the old tail is in interphase. [pause] Why?
A2b.O2.hint: [helpful] Compare with the new tail tip: [pause] which one is still growing?
A2b.O2.optDone: The old tail has finished growing, so few cells are dividing.
A2b.O2.fbDone: [pleased] Finished tissue does its job instead of growing, so most cells stay in interphase. [pause] The growing tip has more dividing cells.
A2b.O2.optDead: Cells in interphase are resting and not doing anything.
A2b.O2.fbDead: [gently] Interphase cells are busy: [pause] they do their jobs, and they grow and copy their DNA when they are getting ready to divide.
A2b.O2.optFast: Interphase is very fast in old tissue.
A2b.O2.fbFast: [gently] If interphase were fast, few cells would be caught in it. [pause] Almost all are.
A2b.O2.optDiffDna: Old-tail cells have different DNA from new-tail cells.
A2b.O2.fbDiffDna: [gently] Every cell in Fig has the same DNA, made by mitosis.
A2b.onion.body: [warm] Onion root tips grow fast, like Fig's new tail. [pause] Count a slice of root tip the same way.
A2b.N1.prompt: [warm] Sort every cell in the onion root tip, then check.
A2b.N2.fb.correct: [pleased] Right. [pause] The same method works for any growing tissue.
A2b.check.body: [encouraging] Three questions about the cell cycle. [pause] Show what you know on your own: hints are off.
A2b.C1.prompt: [curious] In a slice of a growing leaf, thirty of thirty-six cells are in interphase. [pause] What does this tell you?
A2b.C1.fbFast: [gently] More cells in a phase means a longer phase, not a faster one.
A2b.C1.optRest: Most of these cells are resting and doing nothing.
A2b.C1.fbRest: [gently] Interphase cells grow, work and copy their DNA.
A2b.C1.optLong: Cells spend most of their cycle in interphase.
A2b.C1.fbLong: [pleased] Most cells are caught in interphase because it takes most of the cycle.
A2b.C1.fbBroken: [gently] Six cells are dividing, so the leaf cells can divide.
A2b.C2.prompt: [curious] In a slice of root tip, six of forty-eight cells are in metaphase. The cycle takes twenty-four hours. [pause] About how long is metaphase?
A2b.C2.fb6: [gently] Six is the number of cells. [pause] Six divided by forty-eight is the share: one eighth.
mis.percentIsCount: The number of cells is the same as the share of cells.
A2b.C2.fb3: [pleased] Six divided by forty-eight equals one eighth, and one eighth of twenty-four hours is three hours.
A2b.C2.fb12: [gently] Twelve point five is the percent. [pause] Hours are twelve point five percent of twenty-four, not of one hundred.
mis.hoursIsPercent: The percent is the number of hours.
A2b.C2.fb8: [gently] Check the share: [pause] six divided by forty-eight is one eighth, so one eighth of twenty-four hours.
mis.hoursNotScaled: The hours don't depend on the length of the cycle.
A2b.C3.prompt: [curious] On one slide, phase A has nine cells and phase B has two cells. [pause] Which phase lasts longer?
A2b.C3.fbA: [pleased] More cells caught in a phase means cells spend longer in it.
A2b.C3.fbB: [gently] Fewer cells means cells pass through quickly: [pause] phase B is shorter.
A2b.C3.fbSame: [gently] Equal times would give about equal counts.
A2b.C3.optCannot: You cannot tell from a slide.
A2b.C3.fbCannot: [gently] A slide is a snapshot of many cells at once, so the counts estimate the times.
A2b.end.body1: [warm] The cell cycle is continuous. [pause] Cells spend most of it in interphase, growing, working and copying their DNA; mitosis is the short part.
A2b.end.body2: [warm] Growing tissue has more dividing cells than finished tissue, and the share of cells in a phase estimates the share of time. [pause] Next: same DNA, different cells.
A3.R1.prompt: [curious] In a slice of a growing tail tip, why are more cells dividing than in an old tail?
A3.R2.prompt: [curious] After mitosis, how does the DNA in the two new cells compare with the parent?
A3.R4.prompt: [curious] Name two kinds of tissue in Fig's tail.
A3.stump.body1: [warm] At the stump, cells divide by mitosis and make a lump of new cells. [pause] Every one of them has exactly the same chromosomes.
A3.stump.body2: [warm] Look at the count strip: same information as the parent. [pause] So how do some become bone and others skin?
A3.T1.prompt: [warm] Here is one cell from the lump. Try to make it into a bone cell. [pause] Switch genes on and off, then check.
A3.T1.fb.correct: [pleased] A bone cell: only the bone gene is switched on. [pause] The chromosomes did not change at all.
A3.fb.none: [gently] No genes are switched on, so the cell is still undecided. [pause] Switch on the gene for the kind of cell you want.
mis.undecidedIsDone: A cell with no tissue genes switched on is finished.
A3.fb.wrong: [gently] That gene makes a different kind of cell. [pause] Every cell has all three genes: choose which one to switch on.
mis.genesAdded: A cell becomes a new type by gaining new genes.
A3.fb.extra: [gently] More than one gene is switched on, so the cell is mixed up. [pause] A finished cell uses only the genes for its own job.
mis.allGenesOn: A cell switches on all of its genes.
A3.trick.body1: [warm] Every cell in Fig has every gene. [pause] A bone cell switches on the bone gene; a muscle cell, the muscle gene; a skin cell, the skin gene.
A3.trick.body2: [warm] Look at the chromosomes under each cell: they are identical. [pause] Only the switched-on gene (glowing) is different.
A3.G1.prompt: [warm] Make this cell into a muscle cell.
A3.G1.step1: [teacherly] Find the muscle gene and switch it on.
A3.G1.step2: [teacherly] Make sure the other genes are switched off, then check.
A3.hint1: [helpful] Each kind of cell uses the gene for its own job.
A3.hint2: [helpful] Only one tissue gene should be on. [pause] Switching a gene does not add or remove any DNA.
A3.G1.fb.correct: [pleased] A muscle cell: [pause] same chromosomes, with the muscle gene switched on.
A3.I1.prompt: [warm] Make this cell into a skin cell, with Fig's orange colour.
A3.I1.fb.correct: [pleased] A skin cell. [pause] Three cell types so far, all from the same chromosomes.
A3.I2.prompt: [warm] Compare the DNA in one of Fig's skin cells and one of her bone cells.
A3.I2.hint: [helpful] Both cells came from the same lump, by mitosis.
A3.I2.optDiffDna: Different DNA: skin DNA and bone DNA.
A3.I2.fbDiffDna: [gently] Mitosis copies the DNA exactly, so every cell has the same DNA.
mis.differentDnaPerTissue: Each kind of tissue has its own DNA.
A3.I2.optSame: The same DNA, with different genes switched on.
A3.I2.fbSame: [pleased] Same DNA in every cell; what differs is which genes are switched on.
A3.I2.optLost: The skin cell lost its bone genes.
A3.I2.fbLost: [gently] The bone gene is still there in a skin cell, just switched off.
mis.genesLost: Cells lose the genes they don't use.
A3.I2.optHalf: Each has half of Fig's DNA.
A3.I2.fbHalf: [gently] Mitosis gives every cell a full set.
A3.GF.prompt: [curious] Does a muscle cell in Fig's tail still have the skin gene?
A3.GF.optGone: No, it was removed when the cell became muscle.
A3.GF.fbGone: [gently] Nothing is removed. [pause] The skin gene is still on the chromosome, switched off.
A3.GF.optThere: Yes, but it is switched off.
A3.GF.fbThere: [pleased] Every cell keeps every gene. [pause] A muscle cell just doesn't use the skin gene.
A3.GF.optOther: No, muscle cells have muscle DNA.
A3.GF.fbOther: [gently] All of Fig's cells have the same DNA.
A3.GF.optMutant: Only if the cell has a mutation.
A3.GF.fbMutant: [gently] No mutation is needed: [pause] the gene is there in every cell.
A3.regrow.body: [warm] Mitosis made enough cells; switching genes on made them bone, muscle and skin. [pause] Step through the regrowth again.
A3.P1.prompt: [curious] In the cold open, you predicted where Fig's body got the instructions to build a new tail. Read your prediction. [pause] What would you change or add now?
frame.revise: [encouraging] Now I think the instructions came from blank, and the cells became different because blank.
A3.check.body: [encouraging] Three questions about how cells become different. [pause] Show what you know on your own: hints are off.
A3.C1.prompt: [curious] A person's liver cell and nerve cell look and act very differently. [pause] Which is true about their genes?
A3.C1.optLiverMore: The liver cell has extra genes the nerve cell does not.
A3.C1.fbLiverMore: [gently] Every cell has the same genes; none gets extra.
A3.C1.fbDifferent: [gently] Cells in one body have the same DNA, made by mitosis.
A3.C1.optSame: They have the same genes, but use different ones.
A3.C1.fbSame: [pleased] Same genes in both; each switches on the ones for its job.
A3.C1.optNoGenes: The nerve cell has no genes left.
A3.C1.fbNoGenes: [gently] Every cell keeps all its genes.
A3.C2.prompt: [warm] Make this cell into a skin cell.
A3.C2.fb.correct: [pleased] Skin gene on, the others off.
A3.C3.prompt: [curious] Why is a muscle cell not a skin cell?
A3.C3.optSwitched: It has the muscle gene switched on and the skin gene switched off.
A3.C3.fbSwitched: [pleased] Same genes, different ones switched on.
A3.C3.optMutation: A mutation turned its skin gene into a muscle gene.
A3.C3.fbMutation: [gently] No mutation is needed: [pause] both genes are in every cell.
A3.C3.optFewer: It has fewer chromosomes than a skin cell.
A3.C3.fbFewer: [gently] Mitosis gives every cell the same chromosomes.
A3.C3.optParent: It came from a different parent cell with different DNA.
A3.C3.fbParent: [gently] All the cells came from the same lump, with the same DNA.
A3.end.body1: [warm] Every cell has the same DNA, copied by mitosis. [pause] Cells become bone, muscle or skin by switching on different genes.
A3.end.body2: [warm] That is how Fig rebuilt her tail. [pause] Next: where this model is wrong.
A4.R1.prompt: [curious] An X-shaped chromosome: [pause] how many chromosomes, and how many DNA molecules?
A4.R3.prompt: [curious] Why do most cells on a slide look like they are in interphase?
A4.R4.prompt: [curious] How can a bone cell and a skin cell have the same DNA but be different?
A4.limits.body1: [warm] Every model leaves things out. [pause] The card shows what ours simplifies, and what is really true.
A4.limits.body2: [warm] Leaving things out is what makes a model useful: it shows the main idea clearly. [pause] The trick is knowing what was left out.
A4.L1.prompt: [curious] Which is a real way our model newt is different from a real newt?
A4.L1.hint: [helpful] Look at the first row of the card.
A4.L1.optMore: Real newts have many more chromosomes.
A4.L1.fbMore: [pleased] Our newt has four to keep the counting simple; real newts have many more.
A4.L1.fbNoCopy: [gently] Real cells copy their chromosomes before mitosis too; the model got that part right.
A4.L1.optLabels: Real chromosomes are labelled M and P.
A4.L1.fbLabels: [gently] The labels are a model trick. [pause] Real chromosomes are not coloured or labelled.
mis.labelsAreReal: Real chromosomes come labelled and coloured.
A4.L1.fbHalf: [gently] Real mitosis keeps the full set, just like the model.
A4.L2.prompt: [curious] "Share of cells equals share of time" only works if which is true?
A4.L2.hint: [helpful] Look at the timing row of the card.
A4.L2.optSame: Every phase takes the same time.
A4.L2.fbSame: [gently] If phases took the same time, the counts would be equal; the method is for when they differ.
A4.L2.optRandom: Cells divide at random, independent times.
A4.L2.fbRandom: [pleased] If cells were in step with each other, a slide would catch them all in one phase.
A4.L2.optFast: Phases with more cells are faster.
A4.L2.fbFast: [gently] More cells means a longer phase, not a faster one.
A4.L2.fbRest: [gently] Interphase cells are busy, and that is not what makes the method work.
A4.check.body1: [encouraging] Five questions about new situations. [pause] Show what you know on your own: hints, worked steps and sentence starters are off.
A4.check.body2: [encouraging] Your first answer counts. [pause] The last question asks you to explain in your own words; your teacher will read it.
A4.C1.prompt: [warm] This cell comes from a sea star's arm, which is regrowing. [pause] Divide it so both new cells match the parent.
A4.C1.fb.correct: [pleased] Both new cells match the parent.
A4.C2.prompt: [curious] You cut your finger. New skin cells fill the cut. [pause] How does their DNA compare with the skin cells next to the cut?
A4.C2.optHalf: They have half as much DNA.
A4.C2.fbHalf: [gently] Mitosis gives each new cell a full set.
A4.C2.optNeighbour: The same DNA as the cells next to them.
A4.C2.fbNeighbour: [pleased] The new cells were made by mitosis, so they have the same DNA.
A4.C2.optNew: New genes for healing were added.
A4.C2.fbNew: [gently] No genes are added; healing uses the genes every cell already has.
A4.C2.optBlood: They copy DNA from the blood.
A4.C2.fbBlood: [gently] Each new cell gets its DNA by mitosis from the cell that divided.
A4.C3.prompt: [curious] A plant's root cells and leaf cells look very different. [pause] Which is the best explanation?
A4.C3.optLost: Root cells lost their leaf genes.
A4.C3.fbLost: [gently] Root cells keep every gene; the leaf genes are switched off.
A4.C3.optDiff: Roots and leaves have different DNA.
A4.C3.fbDiff: [gently] A plant's cells all have the same DNA, made by mitosis.
A4.C3.optSwitched: They have the same genes, but different genes are switched on.
A4.C3.fbSwitched: [pleased] Same genes everywhere; root and leaf cells switch on different ones.
A4.C3.optSun: Sunlight adds new genes to the leaves.
A4.C3.fbSun: [gently] Light does not add genes; leaf cells use genes they already have.
A4.C4.prompt: [curious] Two skin slides: slide X, from a healing wound, has fourteen of thirty-six cells dividing; slide Y, from healthy skin, has two of thirty-six. [pause] Which came from the part that is growing faster?
A4.C4.fbX: [pleased] More dividing cells means more mitosis, so faster growth: [pause] healing tissue.
A4.C4.fbY: [gently] Fewer dividing cells means slower growth.
A4.C4.optSame: Both are growing at the same rate.
A4.C4.fbSame: [gently] The counts are very different, so the growth is too.
A4.C4.fbNeither: [gently] Skin cells divide all the time to replace old ones, faster in a wound.
A4.C5.prompt: [warm] In your own words: how can a body rebuild a lost part, like Fig's tail? [pause] Use the words mitosis, DNA and genes.
A4.end.body1: [warm] You used a model of chromosomes, mitosis and gene switches to explain how a body grows and repairs itself.
A4.end.body2: [warm] Models leave things out; knowing what they leave out is part of using them well.
A-end.body1: [warm] Mitosis builds and repairs Fig, and every cell it makes has the same DNA. [pause] The life cycle shows where that happens.
A-end.body2: [warm] The grey half (making eggs and sperm, and fertilisation) is Part B. [pause] Something about it is going to surprise everyone.
A-end.done.body1: [warm] Every cell in Fig's body has the same DNA: [pause] mitosis copies it faithfully, and genes switched on or off make bone, muscle and skin.
A-end.done.body2: [warm] Hold that thought. [pause] In Part B, a DNA test says Fig is not the mother of her own hatchlings.
B0.title.body: [warm] Breeding season at Mossbank. [pause] Six hatchlings, one routine DNA test, and a result nobody expected.
B0.story1.body: [warm] Barty and Fig are the only adults in the breeding tank.
B0.story2.body: [warm] A DNA profile shows bands. [pause] A parent and a young newt share one band in every marker, because the young newt got half its DNA from each parent.
B0.T1.prompt: [warm] Mark every band in Hatchling two's lane that matches a band in Barty's lane.
B0.T1.step1: [teacherly] Find Hatchling two's lane and Barty's lane. [pause] Each lane has two bands in every marker.
B0.T1.step2: [teacherly] Look at marker one. [pause] Hatchling two's lower band sits at the same height as one of Barty's bands: that band matches.
B0.T1.step3: [teacherly] Do the same for every marker. [pause] A father matches once in each marker.
B0.T1.hint1: [helpful] Go one marker at a time. [pause] Is either of Hatchling two's bands at the same height as a Barty band?
B0.T1.hint2: [helpful] There is exactly one match in every marker: [pause] six in all.
B0.T1.fb.correct: [pleased] One band from Barty in every marker. [pause] Half of Hatchling two's DNA came from him: Barty is the father.
gel.fb.missed: [gently] Some matching bands aren't marked yet. [pause] Check each marker again.
gel.fb.extra: [gently] A marked band doesn't match. [pause] A band only matches if it sits at exactly the same height, in the same marker.
mis.b.band-near-match: Bands that are close in height count as a match.
B0.T2.prompt: [warm] Now mark every band in Hatchling two's lane that matches Fig's tail clip.
B0.T2.hint1: [helpful] Compare Hatchling two with Fig's tail clip, one marker at a time.
B0.T2.fb.correct: [pleased] Only one band matches, in marker three. [pause] A mother should match once in every marker, so this test says Fig is not the mother.
B0-T3.prompt: [curious] Five of Hatchling two's bands match neither Barty nor Fig's tail clip. [pause] Where must those bands have come from?
B0-T3.opt.mother: From the hatchling's mother, whoever she is.
B0-T3.fb.mother: [pleased] Every hatchling gets half its DNA from its mother. [pause] Those bands are the mother's half.
B0-T3.opt.itself: The hatchling made new DNA for itself.
B0-T3.fb.itself: [gently] Young animals don't make new DNA; they get it all from their parents.
mis.b.dna-from-nowhere: Young animals make new DNA for themselves.
B0-T3.opt.barty: From Barty, but they changed on the way.
B0-T3.fb.barty: [gently] Barty's half already matched, one band per marker. [pause] These are the other half.
mis.b.all-from-father: All of a hatchling's DNA can come from one parent.
B0-T3.opt.broken: Nowhere: the test must be broken.
B0-T3.fb.broken: [gently] Barty's matches came from the same test, and they worked perfectly.
mis.b.test-error: A surprising result means the test is wrong.
B0-P1.prompt: [warm] Tomás thinks someone swapped the eggs. What do you think could explain the test? [pause] Write your best idea.
B0.P1.frame: [encouraging] I think the test says Fig is not the mother because blank.
B1.body: [warm] The evidence board is empty. [pause] Start with what you already know from Part A.
B1-R2.prompt: [curious] Fig's cells have two pairs of chromosomes. [pause] Where did the two chromosomes of a pair come from?
B1-R3.prompt: [curious] An X-shaped chromosome: [pause] how many DNA molecules does it hold?
B1-R4.prompt: [curious] A tail cell and a skin cell from Fig: same DNA or different? [pause] Why?
B1.end.body1: [encouraging] Every body cell has the same DNA, because mitosis copies it exactly. [pause] A hatchling gets half its DNA from each parent.
B1.end.body2: [encouraging] So if Fig is the mother, Hatchling two should match her in every marker. It doesn't. [pause] Something in that reasoning has to give.
B2-R1.prompt: [curious] How much of Hatchling two's DNA came from Barty?
B2-R2.prompt: [curious] What does mitosis do to the number of chromosomes?
B2.meiosis.body1: [warm] Watch one of Fig's egg-making cells. [pause] It copies its chromosomes, then divides twice, so each new cell gets one chromosome from every pair.
B2.meiosis.body2: [warm] Keep an eye on the counts: [pause] four chromosomes in the starting cell, two in each new cell.
B2.G1.prompt: [warm] Make one egg from Fig's egg-making cell.
B2.G1.step1: [teacherly] Pair one has two versions: the one from Fig's mother (A, E) and the one from her father (a, e). An egg gets one of them. [pause] Pick either.
B2.G1.step2: [teacherly] Do the same for pair two: [pause] one of B or b.
B2.G1.step3: [teacherly] Check: one chromosome from each pair, two in all. [pause] That is half of Fig's four.
B2.G1.hint1: [helpful] An egg gets one chromosome from every pair: [pause] not both, and not none.
B2.G1.hint2: [helpful] Fig has two pairs, so an egg has two chromosomes.
B2.G1.fb.correct: [pleased] One from each pair: two chromosomes. [pause] When this egg meets a sperm with two more, the hatchling has four.
gamete.fb.full-set: [gently] That is all of them: a full set. [pause] If eggs and sperm had full sets, the young would end up with twice as many chromosomes as their parents.
mis.b.gamete-full-set: Eggs and sperm get a full set of chromosomes, like body cells.
gamete.fb.both-of-pair: [gently] This one has both chromosomes of a pair and is missing another pair. [pause] Every pair must send exactly one.
mis.b.gamete-both-of-pair: An egg or sperm can get both chromosomes of a pair.
gamete.fb.missing-pair: [gently] One pair has no chromosome here. [pause] Every pair must send one, or the young would be missing those genes.
mis.b.gamete-missing-pair: An egg or sperm can leave out a whole pair.
B2.I1.prompt: [warm] Make one sperm from Barty's sperm-making cell.
B2.I1.hint1: [helpful] Same rule as for eggs: [pause] one chromosome from every pair.
B2.I1.fb.correct: [pleased] A sperm with one chromosome from each pair: [pause] half of Barty's set.
B2.shuffle.body1: [warm] Which chromosome from each pair goes into an egg is down to chance. [pause] Here, the mother's pair one went with the father's pair two.
B2.shuffle.body2: [warm] Before they separate, partners swap matching sections. [pause] Look at pair one: each swapped tip has the other parent's paper and gene letter.
B2.I2.prompt: [warm] Leaving crossing over aside, how many different eggs can Fig's cell make? [pause] Make every different one.
B2.I2.hint1: [helpful] Change one choice at a time: [pause] keep pair one the same and switch pair two.
B2.I2.hint2: [helpful] Pair one has two choices, and so does pair two.
B2.I2.fb.correct: [pleased] Four different eggs: two choices for pair one times two choices for pair two. [pause] Every extra pair doubles the number.
gamete.fb.duplicate.egg: [gently] You already made that egg. [pause] Try a different mix.
B2-I3.prompt: [warm] After crossing over in pair one, how many different versions of chromosome one can end up in Fig's eggs? ( [pause] (Before: A with E, and a with e.
B2-I3.fb.two: [gently] Crossing over adds two new versions: [pause] A with e, and a with E.
mis.b.crossing-over-new-genes: Crossing over makes brand-new genes (or makes nothing new).
B2-I3.fb.four: [pleased] A with E, a with e, and the two swapped versions: [pause] A with e, and a with E.
B2-I3.fb.one: [gently] Meiosis doesn't copy one version into every egg; each egg gets one of several.
mis.b.meiosis-is-copy: Meiosis makes identical copies, like mitosis.
B2-I3.opt.new: Too many to count: it makes brand-new genes.
B2-I3.fb.new: [gently] Crossing over swaps sections between partners. [pause] It mixes genes that are already there.
B2-I3gf.prompt: [warm] Real newts have about twelve pairs of chromosomes. Leaving crossing over aside, how many different eggs could one newt make? (two times two [pause] (two times two times two ...
B2-I3gf.fb.24: [gently] Each pair doubles the number; it doesn't add two. [pause] Two multiplied by itself twelve times is four,ninety-six.
mis.b.combos-add: Each new pair adds two combinations, instead of doubling them.
B2-I3gf.fb.4096: [pleased] Two choices for each of twelve pairs: [pause] four,ninety-six different eggs, before crossing over adds even more.
B2-I3gf.fb.12: [gently] Each pair doesn't make its own kind of egg; every egg has one chromosome from every pair.
mis.b.one-egg-per-pair: Each pair of chromosomes makes its own kind of egg.
B2.fert.body1: [warm] An egg (two chromosomes) and a sperm (two) join into one cell with four: a full set again. [pause] In the hatchling, every chromosome from the egg counts as a mother's chromosome.
B2.fert.body2: [warm] Three siblings, three different eggs and sperm: [pause] same parents, different shuffle.
B2.C1.prompt: [warm] A moth's egg-making cell has three pairs of chromosomes. [pause] Make one egg.
B2.C1.fb.correct: [pleased] One from each of the three pairs: [pause] three chromosomes, half of the moth's six.
B2-C2.prompt: [curious] Two kittens have the same mother and father but look different. [pause] Which is the best explanation?
B2-C2.opt.blend: Each kitten blends its parents in a different amount, like mixing paint.
B2-C2.fb.blend: [gently] Kittens don't get a blend; each gets a full set of chromosomes, one from each pair, from each parent.
mis.b.blending: Children are a blend of their parents, like mixed paint.
B2-C2.opt.shuffle: Each kitten came from a different egg and sperm, shuffled differently in meiosis.
B2-C2.fb.shuffle: [pleased] Meiosis shuffles chromosomes and swaps sections, so every egg and sperm is different.
B2-C2.opt.same: They got the same chromosomes; food made them look different.
B2-C2.fb.same: [gently] Siblings don't get the same chromosomes; each egg and sperm carries a different mix.
mis.b.siblings-identical: Children of the same parents get the same chromosomes.
B2-C2.opt.copy: Meiosis copies the parents exactly, so one kitten must have different parents.
B2-C2.fb.copy: [gently] Meiosis halves and shuffles; it doesn't copy. [pause] Different-looking siblings are normal.
B2.end.body1: [warm] Meiosis halves the chromosomes and shuffles them, so every egg and sperm is one of a kind.
B2.end.body2: [warm] That shuffle is the first source of new variation: [pause] new combinations of the parents' genes.
B3-R1.prompt: [curious] How many chromosomes does one of Fig's eggs have?
B3-R2.prompt: [curious] Give one reason why no two eggs are the same.
B3-R3.prompt: [curious] What does a cell do to its chromosomes before it divides?
B3-P1.prompt: [warm] Mitosis and meiosis start with the same cell. [pause] Predict two ways the new cells will be different.
B3.P1.frame: [encouraging] Mitosis makes blank. [pause] Meiosis makes blank.
B3.side.body1: [warm] Step through both at once and read the counts under each side.
B3.side.body2: [warm] Mitosis copies, then divides once. [pause] Meiosis copies, then divides twice, shuffling and swapping along the way.
B3-G1.prompt: [curious] Sort each statement: [pause] is it true of mitosis, meiosis, or both?
B3.G1.hint1: [helpful] Step through the animation again and read the counts under each side.
B3.G1.hint2: [helpful] Only one of them swaps sections and halves the chromosomes. [pause] Both copy first.
B3-G1.item.same: The new cells are identical to the parent cell.
B3-G1.item.half: Each new cell gets one chromosome from every pair.
mis.b.swap-in-mitosis: Mitosis also swaps sections between partners.
B3-G1.item.body: Builds and repairs the body, like Fig's tail.
B3-G1.fb.correct: [pleased] All sorted. [pause] Mitosis copies; meiosis halves and shuffles; both start by copying.
B3-I1.prompt: [curious] A cell with six chromosomes (three pairs) goes through meiosis. [pause] How many chromosomes are in each new cell?
B3-I1.fb.six: [gently] That would be mitosis. [pause] Meiosis gives each new cell one chromosome from every pair.
B3-I1.fb.three: [pleased] One from each of the three pairs: [pause] half the chromosomes.
B3-I1.fb.twelve: [gently] Copying makes each chromosome an X, but it is still one chromosome. [pause] Then meiosis halves the number.
B3-I1.fb.two: [gently] Each new cell needs one chromosome from every pair, and there are three pairs.
B3-C1.prompt: [curious] A skin cell divides to heal a scrape. A cell in an ovary divides to make eggs. [pause] Which statement is true?
B3-C1.opt.both-same: Both make cells identical to the parent.
B3-C1.fb.both-same: [gently] Eggs are made by meiosis, which halves and shuffles.
B3-C1.opt.both-half: Both halve the number of chromosomes.
B3-C1.fb.both-half: [gently] Healing uses mitosis, which keeps the full set.
B3-C1.opt.right: The new skin cells are identical to the parent; the eggs all differ from each other.
B3-C1.fb.right: [pleased] Mitosis copies (skin); meiosis halves and shuffles (eggs).
B3-C1.opt.swapped: The new skin cells all differ; the eggs are identical.
B3-C1.fb.swapped: [gently] That is the wrong way round: [pause] mitosis makes identical cells, meiosis makes different ones.
mis.b.mitosis-shuffles: Mitosis makes cells that are all different.
B3-C2.prompt: [warm] Look back at your prediction. In your own words: how is meiosis different from mitosis? [pause] Give two differences.
B3.end.body1: [warm] Mitosis makes two cells identical to the parent: it builds and repairs the body. [pause] Meiosis makes four cells with half the chromosomes, all different: eggs or sperm.
B3.end.body2: [warm] Both start by copying the chromosomes. [pause] What happens next is the difference.
B4-R2.prompt: [curious] In the DNA test, which adult matched Hatchling two?
B4-R3.prompt: [curious] Why do a bone cell and a skin cell from the same newt have the same DNA?
B4.intro.body: [warm] Each tank shows one way new variation can appear. [pause] Watch where the change happens: in a body cell, or in a cell that makes eggs.
B4.L1.prompt: [warm] Run all three tanks. [pause] For each one, find where the change happens and whether it reaches the hatchlings.
B4.L1.hint1: [helpful] After each run, find the star: that is where the change happened. [pause] Then follow the arrows to the hatchlings.
B4.card.shuffle: [warm] Tank one: meiosis shuffles chromosomes, so every egg is different. [pause] New mixes are passed on.
B4.card.copy: [warm] Tank two: a copying error in an egg-making cell gave Hatchling five a white tail tip. [pause] Passed on.
B4.card.uv: [warm] Tank three: UV light changed a patch of skin. Her young had normal skin. [pause] Not passed on.
B4.lab.fb.done: [pleased] All three tanks are in the evidence locker. [pause] Two kinds of change reached the young; one didn't.
B4.rule.body1: [warm] A change in a body cell, like skin, stays in that newt. [pause] It never reaches the eggs.
B4.rule.body2: [warm] A change in an egg-making or sperm-making cell can end up in the young. [pause] So can the new mixes that meiosis makes.
B4-G1.prompt: [curious] Sort each change: [pause] can it be passed on to the young, or not?
B4.G1.hint1: [helpful] Ask: [pause] is the change in a cell that makes eggs or sperm?
B4.G1.hint2: [helpful] What caused the change doesn't matter. [pause] Where it happened does.
B4-G1.item.mix: A new mix of chromosomes in an egg (the shuffle).
B4-G1.item.sperm: A copying error in a sperm-making cell.
mis.b.environment-never-inherited: Changes caused by the environment can never be passed on.
B4-G1.item.uv: A patch of skin changed by UV light.
mis.b.all-changes-inherited: Any change in the body gets passed on to the young.
B4-G1.item.tail: A copying error in a tail cell while the tail regrows.
B4-G1.item.legs: Strong legs from a newt that swims a lot.
mis.b.acquired-traits: Traits a parent gains during life get passed on.
B4-G1.item.uvgerm: UV damage to an egg-making cell.
B4-G1.fb.correct: [pleased] All sorted. [pause] Only changes in egg- or sperm-making cells, and new mixes from meiosis, reach the young.
B4-I1.prompt: [curious] A fisher gets a sun-damaged patch of skin after years outdoors. [pause] Will their children inherit the change?
B4-I1.opt.all: Yes: every change in the body is passed on.
B4-I1.fb.all: [gently] Only changes in cells that make eggs or sperm can be passed on.
B4-I1.opt.long: Yes, if the change lasts long enough.
B4-I1.fb.long: [gently] How long it lasts doesn't matter; skin cells never make eggs or sperm.
B4-I1.opt.skin: No: skin cells don't make eggs or sperm.
B4-I1.fb.skin: [pleased] The change is in skin cells, so it stays with the fisher.
B4-I1.opt.never: No: changes caused by the sun can never be inherited.
B4-I1.fb.never: [gently] Right answer, wrong reason. [pause] Sun damage to egg- or sperm-making cells could be inherited; here it hit skin.
B4-C1.prompt: [curious] A mouse is born with curly fur, though both parents have straight fur and no relative has ever had curly fur. [pause] Which explanation is most likely?
B4-C1.opt.learned: The mother's fur turned curly during her life and she passed it on.
B4-C1.fb.learned: [gently] Changes during a parent's life aren't passed on unless they happen in egg- or sperm-making cells.
B4-C1.opt.blend: Straight fur from two parents blended into curly fur.
B4-C1.fb.blend: [gently] Traits don't blend like paint, and straight plus straight has no curly to blend.
B4-C1.opt.copy: A copying error in an egg-making or sperm-making cell of one parent.
B4-C1.fb.copy: [pleased] A new change in a cell that makes eggs or sperm can show up in the young.
B4-C1.opt.skin: Sun damage to the father's skin cells.
B4-C1.fb.skin: [gently] Skin cells don't make sperm, so their changes stay in the father.
B4.end.body1: [warm] New variation that can be inherited comes from three places: [pause] new mixes made by meiosis, copying errors in egg- or sperm-making cells, and changes caused by the environment in those cells.
B4.end.body2: [warm] A change only reaches the young if it is in the cells that make eggs or sperm.
B5-R1.prompt: [curious] Which changes can be passed on to the young?
B5-R2.prompt: [curious] In meiosis, what does each egg get?
B5-R3.prompt: [curious] How exactly does mitosis copy DNA?
B5.night.body: [warm] Fig laid the eggs: the camera saw it. The test says she isn't the mother. [pause] Time to test more of Fig.
B5.T1.prompt: [warm] Choose which parts of Fig to test. [pause] Test her egg cells and at least one other tissue.
B5.T1.hint1: [helpful] Test the egg cells and at least one other part of Fig, then compare each new lane with Hatchling two.
B5.T1.fb.correct: [pleased] Fig's body samples match each other but not Hatchling two. [pause] Her egg cells match Hatchling two in every marker.
gel.result.figTail: [warm] Tail clip: [pause] does not match Hatchling two (Ada ran it twice: same bands both times).
gel.result.figSkin: [warm] Skin: the same bands as the tail clip. [pause] Does not match Hatchling two.
gel.result.figBlood: [warm] Blood: the same bands as the tail clip. [pause] Does not match Hatchling two.
gel.result.figEggs: [warm] Egg cells: [pause] a match for Hatchling two in every marker (run twice: same result).
B5-I1.prompt: [curious] Which of Fig's samples could have come from the hatchlings' mother?
B5-I1.fb.tail: [gently] The tail clip shares only one band with Hatchling two.
mis.b.dna-same-everywhere: Every cell in one body always has the same DNA.
B5-I1.fb.blood: [gently] Blood has the same bands as the tail: no match.
B5-I1.fb.eggs: [pleased] The egg cells match Hatchling two in every marker.
B5-I1.opt.none: None: the eggs must have been swapped.
B5-I1.fb.none: [gently] Fig's own egg cells match. [pause] No swap is needed to explain it.
mis.b.eggs-swapped: The eggs must have come from another newt.
B5.reveal.body: [warm] Fig's body and Fig's egg cells have different DNA.
B5.lines.body1: [warm] Long before Fig hatched, two embryos fused into one. [pause] Each line of cells kept copying itself exactly, by mitosis.
B5.lines.body2: [warm] Line one built her tail, skin and blood. [pause] Line two built the cells that make her eggs, so only line two reaches the hatchlings.
B5-I2.prompt: [curious] Why did the tail-clip test say Fig was not the mother?
B5-I2.opt.machine: The DNA machine made a mistake.
B5-I2.fb.machine: [gently] Ada ran the tail twice and got the same bands; skin and blood agree too.
B5-I2.opt.mutation: One mutation changed the hatchlings' DNA.
B5-I2.fb.mutation: [gently] One copying error changes one place; Hatchling two differs in five of six markers.
mis.b.one-mutation: One mutation can explain many differences at once.
B5-I2.opt.lines: Her tail was built by a different cell line than her eggs.
B5-I2.fb.lines: [pleased] The tail comes from line one; her eggs come from line two.
B5-I2.fb.swap: [gently] Fig's own egg cells match the hatchlings, and the camera saw her lay them.
B5-C1.prompt: [curious] A chimera cat's fur is made by one cell line and its eggs by another. [pause] To find out what its kittens could inherit, which sample should you test?
B5-C1.fb.fur: [gently] Fur comes from the other line, which the kittens don't inherit.
B5-C1.fb.blood: [gently] Blood could come from either line; only the egg-making line is inherited.
B5-C1.fb.eggs: [pleased] Only the egg-making line passes DNA to the kittens.
B5-C1.opt.any: Any sample: all its cells have the same DNA.
B5-C1.fb.any: [gently] In a chimera, the two cell lines have different DNA.
B5.end.body1: [warm] Fig is a chimera: one body, two cell lines with different DNA. [pause] Mitosis copied each line faithfully.
B5.end.body2: [warm] Only the line that makes her eggs is inherited. [pause] The tail clip just sampled the wrong Fig.
B6-R2.prompt: [curious] Which of Fig's samples matched the hatchlings?
B6-R3.prompt: [curious] What does mitosis do to the DNA in each new cell?
B6.board.body1: [warm] Here is your evidence locker: [pause] the cards you filed in the lab and the tissue tests.
B6.board.body2: [warm] A strong argument has a claim, the evidence for it, and the reasoning that links them. [pause] Then it answers the other side.
B6-G1.prompt: [warm] Write your claim: is Fig the hatchlings' mother? [pause] Add two pieces of evidence from the locker.
B6.G1.frame: [encouraging] I claim that blank. One piece of evidence is blank. Another is blank. [pause] This shows blank because blank.
B6-I1.prompt: [curious] Tomás still says someone swapped the eggs. [pause] Which evidence answers him best?
B6-I1.opt.tank: The hatchlings live in Fig's tank.
B6-I1.fb.tank: [gently] Being in Fig's tank doesn't show where the eggs came from.
mis.b.correlation-is-cause: Two things that happen together must cause each other.
B6-I1.fb.barty: [gently] Barty matching says nothing about who the mother is.
mis.b.one-parent-proves-both: If one parent matches, the other must too.
B6-I1.opt.camera: Camera footage shows Fig laying these eggs, and her egg cells match them.
B6-I1.fb.camera: [pleased] Direct evidence: [pause] she was seen laying them, and her egg-cell DNA matches.
B6-I1.fb.calm: [gently] How a newt acts isn't evidence about DNA.
mis.b.opinion-as-evidence: How someone acts or seems counts as evidence.
B6-I2.prompt: [curious] Noor wonders if the DNA machine made a mistake. [pause] Which evidence answers her best?
B6-I2.opt.repeat: Ada ran the tests again and got the same bands each time.
B6-I2.fb.repeat: [pleased] Repeat runs that agree make a machine error very unlikely.
B6-I2.fb.surprise: [gently] A surprising result is a reason to repeat the test, not to throw it out.
B6-I2.opt.barty: Barty's result was right, so Fig's must be too.
B6-I2.fb.barty: [gently] One result being right doesn't prove another one.
B6-I2.fb.careful: [gently] Trusting a person isn't the same as evidence; repeat runs are.
B6-I3.prompt: [curious] Someone suggests that one mutation in Fig's eggs changed their DNA. [pause] Which evidence answers this best?
B6-I3.fb.anything: [gently] One copying error changes one place in the DNA, not a whole profile.
B6-I3.opt.regrew: Fig's tail regrew, so her DNA must have changed.
B6-I3.fb.regrew: [gently] Regrowth is mitosis, which copies DNA exactly.
B6-I3.opt.five: Hatchling two differs from Fig's tail in five of six markers: far too many for one copying error.
B6-I3.fb.five: [pleased] Five markers differ. [pause] One mutation can't explain that; a second cell line can.
B6-I3.fb.broken: [gently] Repeat runs gave the same bands.
B6-I4.prompt: [curious] The hatchlings hatched in the same week the old UV lamp was repaired. [pause] Does that show the lamp changed their DNA?
B6-I4.opt.yes: Yes: they happened at the same time, so the lamp caused it.
B6-I4.fb.yes: [gently] Two things happening together doesn't show that one caused the other.
B6-I4.opt.no: No: two things happening at the same time doesn't show that one caused the other.
B6-I4.fb.no: [pleased] You would need evidence of how the lamp could have changed them. [pause] The DNA tests already explain the result.
B6-I4.opt.never: No: UV light can never change DNA.
B6-I4.fb.never: [gently] UV can change DNA (Tank three). [pause] The point is that timing alone isn't evidence.
B6-I4.opt.sat: Yes: if the mother sat under the lamp, the young inherit it.
B6-I4.fb.sat: [gently] UV on her skin wouldn't reach the young, and timing alone shows nothing.
B6-C1.prompt: [warm] Write your full argument for Tomás. [pause] Make a claim, give evidence, explain your reasoning, and answer at least one counterclaim.
B6.end.body1: [warm] Fig is the mother. [pause] Her egg-making cells carry a second cell line, and that is the DNA the hatchlings inherited.
B6.end.body2: [warm] Good evidence answers each counterclaim directly: [pause] the camera, the repeat runs, and the number of differences.
B7.body1: [warm] Fig's eggs come from the cell line of her fused twin. [pause] The hatchlings are, genetically, her twin's young: her nieces and nephews.
B7.cycle.body1: [warm] Both halves are filled in now: [pause] meiosis makes eggs and sperm, fertilisation joins them, and mitosis builds the body.
B7.cycle.body2: [warm] Chimeras happen in other animals too, including people. [pause] Usually nobody knows, unless a DNA test gives a surprising answer, just like Fig's.
B7.done.body1: [encouraging] You solved the mystery with evidence: [pause] DNA profiles, the variation lab, and how meiosis and mitosis work.
Bc-R1.prompt: [curious] Why does a regrown tail have the same DNA as the rest of the newt?
Bc-R2.prompt: [curious] How many chromosomes does an egg get, compared with a body cell?
Bc-R3.prompt: [curious] Name three sources of new variation that can be passed on.
Bcheck.intro.body1: [encouraging] Five questions about new situations. [pause] Work on your own: hints, worked steps and sentence starters are off.
Bcheck.intro.body2: [encouraging] Your first answer counts. [pause] The last question asks you to make a claim; your teacher will read it.
Bc.C1.prompt: [warm] A frog's sperm-making cell has three pairs of chromosomes. [pause] Make one sperm.
Bc.C1.fb.correct: [pleased] One chromosome from each of the three pairs: [pause] half of the frog's six.
Bc-C2.prompt: [curious] Two sisters (not twins) have the same parents, but their DNA is different. [pause] Why?
Bc-C2.opt.shuffle: Each came from a different egg and sperm, each with its own shuffle.
Bc-C2.fb.shuffle: [pleased] Meiosis makes every egg and sperm different.
Bc-C2.opt.older: The older sister's DNA changed as she grew up.
Bc-C2.fb.older: [gently] Growing up uses mitosis, which copies DNA exactly.
Bc-C2.opt.same: Their DNA is really the same; tests can't tell them apart.
Bc-C2.fb.same: [gently] Siblings get different mixes; tests can tell them apart.
Bc-C2.opt.blend: Each got a different blend of their parents, like paint.
Bc-C2.fb.blend: [gently] Children get whole chromosomes, one from each pair, not a blend.
Bc-C3.prompt: [curious] Which of these changes could a lizard pass on to its young?
Bc-C3.item.tail: A tail broken off by a cat.
Bc-C3.item.egg: A copying error in a cell that makes eggs.
Bc-C3.item.mix: A new mix of chromosomes made in meiosis.
Bc-C3.fb.correct: [pleased] All sorted: [pause] only changes in egg- or sperm-making cells, and new mixes, reach the young.
Bc-C4.prompt: [curious] A chemical in a pond damages the DNA in a newt's sperm-making cells. [pause] Could the change appear in its young?
Bc-C4.opt.yes: Yes: sperm-making cells make the sperm that become the young.
Bc-C4.fb.yes: [pleased] A change in sperm-making cells can be carried into a sperm and then the young.
Bc-C4.opt.never: No: changes caused by the environment are never inherited.
Bc-C4.fb.never: [gently] The cause doesn't matter; where the change happens does.
Bc-C4.opt.long: Only if the newt lives in the pond for a long time.
Bc-C4.fb.long: [gently] Time in the pond doesn't decide it; whether the sperm carry the change does.
Bc-C4.opt.skin: Yes, and so will every change in its skin.
Bc-C4.fb.skin: [gently] Skin changes stay in the newt.
Bc-C5.prompt: [warm] Two brown rabbits have eight young. One is white, and no rabbit in the family has ever been white. [pause] Make a claim about where this new variation came from, and support it with evidence and reasoning.
Bcheck.end.body1: [warm] You explained where new, inheritable variation comes from: [pause] new mixes in meiosis, copying errors, and changes caused by the environment in egg- or sperm-making cells.
Bcheck.end.body2: [warm] And you know why a change has to be in those cells to be passed on.
